description: Somos un equipo de estudiantes de séptimo grado a bachillerato participando con mucho entusiasmo en el NASA Space Apps Challenge, listos para aprender y crear soluciones espaciales increíbles.
summary:
Our project Senda, is a mission-planning console that helps astronauts and mission controllers plan safe surface walks (EVAs) on Mars. Inspired by open-source intelligence (OSINT) dashboards, Senda layers several NASA datasets on one interactive map, with feeds, a mission log and a site dossier. Planners can compare landing sites on a 3D globe, check terrain slope, shallow water ice, dust (atmospheric opacity τ) and radiation and space weather, and then draw and evaluate a 2 km EVA route for one astronaut supervised by a three-person crew.

Senda works in two settings. The first is Arcadia Planitia, our proposed mission base at 40.1° N, 191.4° E. The second is Gale Crater and Mount Sharp, where we check our approach against what Curiosity has actually done, using its real traverse (MMGIS waypoints), REMS weather data, raw images and NOAA space-weather feeds. The app is bilingual (ES/EN), works on phones and keeps working offline.

This matters because an EVA on Mars leaves no room for error. Senda turns scattered open data into one clear, decision-ready map, from open data to the first footprint.
details:
What it does

Senda is a web console for planning the first human surface walks (EVAs) on Mars. It follows a mission in four stages:

1. Site: compare candidate landing sites on a 3D Mars globe, checked against NASA's exploration rules: stay inside the Exploration Zone, avoid caves, perchlorates and volcanic ground, and never walk slopes over 30°.

2. Landing: see the descent sequence and the landing module in 3D.

3. Walk: plan a 2 km EVA from the Artemis Base in Arcadia Planitia (40.1° N, 191.4° E), where one astronaut walks while three crew members supervise. Users pick stops on a 2D map or a 3D terrain view, such as polygonal ground, a fresh crater with shallow ice or a scarp. Senda then calculates the distance, the duration, the oxygen and energy used, the radiation dose and the minutes back to shelter, and it warns when a plan breaks a safety margin.

4. Live: an OSINT-style dashboard with Curiosity's real position, REMS weather, the latest raw images, NOAA space weather, the Earth–Mars signal delay and a mission log.

How we validate it

We run the same tools in two places. Arcadia Planitia is the mission site, and its terrain is modeled from the features MOLA, THEMIS and SHARAD show for the region. Gale Crater and Mount Sharp is the validation site, where we use the real path Curiosity drove.

Benefits and intended impact

Senda brings data scattered across several NASA and NOAA portals into one clear, decision-ready map. With a signal delay of up to 22 minutes, the crew has to be able to decide on site, and Senda gives them what they need to do that. We want Senda to be a starting point for real EVA planning tools. The next steps are real HiRISE elevation models, CRISM mineral maps, walks with several astronauts and automatic alerts for dust storms and solar events.

How it is creative

We took the style of OSINT (open-source intelligence) dashboards, with layered maps, live feeds, a mission log and a site dossier, and applied it to Mars exploration. We also check our plan against reality: the same tools run where Curiosity actually drove before we trust them where people will walk.

Factors we considered

We considered astronaut safety first: NASA's exploration-zone rules, the 30° slope limit, toxic perchlorates, radiation dose, oxygen and energy reserves and the time needed to get back to shelter. We also considered the Earth–Mars communication delay, the honesty of the data (in the app we label what is real and what is modeled), and accessibility: the app is bilingual, works on phones and works offline.

Tools

HTML, CSS and JavaScript; Three.js for the 3D terrain, globe and module; Python for the build script; GitHub and Vercel for hosting. AI assistance (Claude, by Anthropic) was used for coding, brand graphics and English texts, as disclosed in our README.
